title: The solar system: why a rocky planet and a gas giant are so different, and how we know

summary.text: Mercury is the closest planet to the Sun, yet Venus is hotter. Jupiter is about 11 times as wide as the Earth, yet a lump of Jupiter weighs only about a quarter as much as a lump of Earth the same size, and Saturn is lighter than water. Four planets have solid ground and four have none, though all eight formed from one cloud around one Sun. Your child drops marbles into flour to see how craters give away the age of a world, shakes a jar and watches it settle into layers as a young planet did, finds the rule that links a planet's distance to the length of its year, and walks a model where the Earth is a mustard seed. Along the way: why Mars lost its air, why a day on Venus is longer than its year, and why a message sent to a spacecraft at Mars is already many minutes old when it arrives.
summary.art: A kitchen table with a tray of flour full of marble craters, a jar with layers of steel nuts, sand, water and oil, and a row of eight planets drawn on a long strip of paper behind them.

intro.hook: Four of the eight planets have solid ground. If you dropped a stone on Jupiter, it would never land, because there is no ground to land on. All eight planets formed from the same cloud of gas and dust, around the same young Sun. So why did they turn out as two quite different kinds of world?
intro.text: In this unit you find out. You drop marbles into a tray of flour and learn how scientists read the age of a planet from its craters. You sort heavy things from light things in a jar, the way a young planet sorted itself. You work out how long sunlight takes to reach each planet, and why that makes driving a rover on Mars so slow. You also meet Inge Lehmann, a Danish scientist who found out what is inside the Earth without ever digging a hole.
intro.art: A cut-open Earth showing a bright core, a mantle and a thin crust next to a cut-open Jupiter that is mostly swirling gas, both drawn as if they were fruit sliced in half.

outcomes: I can explain how rocky planets and giant planets differ in size, make-up, density and whether they have solid ground.
I can use density to say which planets are made of rock and metal and which of gas, and why Saturn would float in water.
I can explain how counting craters shows the age of a surface, and why the Moon and Mercury have many craters while the Earth has few.
I can explain how an atmosphere decides how hot a planet is, using Venus, the Earth, Mars and Mercury.
I can find, from data, the rule that links a planet's distance from the Sun to the length of its year.
I can work out how long light takes to travel across the solar system, and say why a message to Mars arrives late.
I can use a scale model to show that the solar system is mostly empty space, with tiny planets very far apart.

terms.meaning: A planet made mostly of rock and metal, with a solid surface you could stand on. It is small, dense and close to the Sun.
terms.example: Mercury, Venus, the Earth and Mars are the four rocky planets.
terms.art: Four small planets side by side, each with a hard, cratered, cloudy or blue-and-white surface.

terms.meaning: A very large planet made mostly of the gases hydrogen and helium. It has no solid surface. Going deeper, the gas just gets thicker and hotter.
terms.example: Jupiter and Saturn are gas giants. They are made of the same gases as the Sun.
terms.art: Jupiter with brown and cream stripes and Saturn with bright rings, both far bigger than a tiny Earth beside them.

terms.meaning: A giant planet made of a lot of water, ammonia and methane, mixed with hydrogen and helium. Scientists call these 'ices' because they freeze solid in the cold far from the Sun. Inside the planet they are hot and fluid.
terms.example: Uranus and Neptune are ice giants. Their blue colour comes from methane in their air.
terms.art: Pale blue-green Uranus and deep blue Neptune, with thin rings, side by side.

terms.meaning: How heavy a thing is for its size. A dense thing packs a lot of material into a small space.
terms.example: A steel nut is much denser than a wooden block of the same size. The Earth is denser than Saturn.
terms.art: Two boxes of the same size, one filled with steel nuts and one with cotton wool, on the two sides of a balance.

terms.meaning: The centre of a planet. The Earth's core is made mostly of iron and nickel, and it is hot and very heavy.
terms.example: The Earth's inner core is solid iron and nickel, about as hot as the surface of the Sun.
terms.art: A cut-open Earth with a small bright ball at the middle, a larger ring of glowing metal around it, and layers of rock outside.

terms.meaning: A bowl-shaped hole made when a rock from space hits a planet or moon. Most craters are round, whichever way the rock came from.
terms.example: The Moon's face is covered with craters. Lonar Lake in Maharashtra fills a crater about 1.8 kilometres wide.
terms.art: A round crater with a raised rim and long pale streaks of thrown-out material spreading from it.

terms.meaning: The layer of gas, or air, held around a planet by the planet's gravity. A thick atmosphere can trap heat. A thin one lets heat escape.
terms.example: Venus has a very thick atmosphere of carbon dioxide. Mercury has almost none.
terms.art: Four planets cut in half, each with a different thickness of air around it, from almost none to a thick yellow blanket.

terms.meaning: The way some gases in the air let sunlight in but slow down the heat trying to leave, so the planet's surface becomes warmer.
terms.example: The greenhouse effect warms the Earth by about 33 degrees Celsius. On Venus, it makes the ground hotter than an oven.
terms.art: Sunlight arriving at a planet as yellow arrows, and orange heat arrows trying to leave but bouncing back from a layer of air.

terms.meaning: A stretched circle, shaped like an oval. Every planet moves round the Sun on a path that is an ellipse, though for most planets it is nearly a circle.
terms.example: You get an ellipse if you tilt a round plate and look at it from the side.
terms.art: A round plate tilted so its rim looks like an oval, next to the Sun with a planet on an oval path.

terms.meaning: The average distance from the Earth to the Sun, which is about 150 million kilometres. Astronomers use it as a measuring stick for the solar system. It is written AU.
terms.example: Jupiter is about 5.2 astronomical units from the Sun. That is 5.2 times as far as the Earth.
terms.art: A ruler with a Sun at one end and the Earth at the 1 mark, Mars at 1.5 and Jupiter far along at 5.2.

terms.meaning: The time light takes to travel from one place to another. Radio signals from spacecraft travel at the same speed as light. Light needs about 8 minutes and 20 seconds to come from the Sun to the Earth.
terms.example: Sunlight takes about 4 hours to reach Neptune. A message to Mars takes between 3 and 22 minutes, depending on where Mars is.
terms.art: A ray of light leaving the Sun with small clocks along the way showing 8 minutes at the Earth and 4 hours at Neptune.

terms.meaning: The distance from the young Sun beyond which water could freeze into ice. Closer in, it was too warm and only rock and metal could be solid.
terms.example: Scientists think the frost line was somewhere between 3 and 5 times as far from the Sun as the Earth. Jupiter formed beyond it.
terms.art: A young Sun with a dusty disc round it, a dotted circle marking the frost line, and ice crystals only outside the circle.

terms.meaning: Spinning round on its own axis, like a top. One full rotation is a day. A day is a different length on each planet.
terms.example: Jupiter rotates once in just under 10 hours. Venus takes 243 Earth days to rotate once.
terms.art: A planet with a line through its middle, a curved arrow showing it spinning, and a small flag on its surface.

terms.meaning: The invisible region round a planet where its magnetism can be felt. The Earth's magnetic field is made by its moving liquid iron core. It helps to turn aside the fast particles blowing out from the Sun.
terms.example: A compass needle points north because of the Earth's magnetic field.
terms.art: The Earth with curved lines of magnetic field bending away a stream of particles from the Sun.

terms.meaning: A smaller copy of something in which every size or distance is made smaller by the same amount. A good model for the solar system must shrink sizes and distances together.
terms.example: A map is a scale model. In a model where the Sun is 14 centimetres wide, the Earth is a 1 millimetre grain 15 metres away.
terms.art: A tiny grain beside a large disc, with a long measuring tape stretching between them.

terms.meaning: An orbiter is a spacecraft that goes round a planet or moon. A rover is a robot vehicle that drives on the surface of another world.
terms.example: India's Mangalyaan was an orbiter at Mars. Curiosity and Perseverance are rovers that drive on Mars.
terms.art: A small spacecraft circling a red planet, and a six-wheeled rover leaving tracks on its dusty surface.

explanations.concept: Rocky planets and giant planets differ in more than size
explanations.definition: The four inner planets are small, dense balls of rock and metal with solid ground. The four outer planets are giants with no ground, made mostly of gases and the 'ices' of water, ammonia and methane.
explanations.description: Mercury, Venus, the Earth and Mars are small, because only rock and metal could stay solid close to the young Sun. Jupiter is about 11 times as wide as the Earth. About 1,300 Earths would fit inside it. Jupiter and Saturn are made mostly of hydrogen and helium, the same gases as the Sun. Uranus and Neptune hold a lot of water, ammonia and methane, and they are called ice giants. A giant has no surface to land on. Going down, the gas gets thicker and hotter until it is more like a hot fluid. When astronomers need a 'surface' for Jupiter, they choose the level where the air pressure equals the pressure at sea level on the Earth.
examples: A spacecraft sent into Jupiter's clouds cannot land. It is crushed and heated long before it could reach anything solid.
Mars has volcanoes and canyons because it has solid ground. Olympus Mons, a volcano on Mars, is about 22 kilometres high. Mount Everest is less than 9 kilometres high.
All four giants have rings, though only Saturn's are bright and wide enough to see with a small telescope.
explanations.art: The four rocky planets drawn as small solid balls beside Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune, with a dotted line showing the depth where a giant's gas turns to hot fluid.
explanations.context: This card explains the biggest split among the planets: four rocky ones with ground, and four giants without.

explanations.concept: Density: how heavy a planet is for its size
explanations.definition: Density is the mass of a thing divided by the space it takes up. Water has a density of 1 gram in every cubic centimetre. A planet with a density below 1 is lighter than the same amount of water.
explanations.description: Astronomers weigh a planet by seeing how strongly its gravity pulls on a moon or a passing spacecraft. They measure its size with a telescope or a camera. Dividing one by the other gives the density. The four rocky planets are all dense. The Earth's density is about 5.5, Mercury's is about 5.4, Venus's about 5.2 and Mars's about 3.9. The giants are light for their size. Jupiter's is about 1.3, Uranus's about 1.3 and Neptune's about 1.6. Saturn's is only about 0.7. So Saturn is lighter than water. If you could find a bathtub big enough, Saturn would float. The Earth is the densest planet in the solar system.
examples: Rock on the Earth's surface has a density of about 3. The whole Earth is denser, at about 5.5, so the middle of the Earth must be much denser than rock. It is iron.
Jupiter weighs about 318 times as much as the Earth but takes up about 1,300 times the space, so it is far less dense.
Mars is the least dense of the rocky planets. It is small, so its own gravity squeezes its rock less.
explanations.art: A bar chart of the eight planets' densities with a thick line at 1 for water, the four rocky planets high above the line and Saturn's bar below it.
explanations.context: This card explains how the planets are told apart by density, which shows what they are made of.

explanations.concept: Why the planets are two kinds: the frost line and the growth of the giants
explanations.description: The planets formed in a flat, spinning disc of gas and dust round the young Sun. Close to the Sun it was warm, and only rock and metal could be solid, so the inner planets stayed small. Beyond the frost line, which was probably about 3 to 5 times as far as the Earth, water could freeze too. There was much more solid stuff to gather, so planets there grew larger. Astronomers agree on this much. They do not agree on how the giants then grew. One idea says a heavy core formed first and then pulled in gas. Another says a clump of the disc collapsed all at once. Both ideas explain some of what we see, and neither explains everything.
examples: Jupiter and Saturn are made of hydrogen and helium, the gases that fill most of the disc. Rocky planets could not hold on to light gases.
Planets are now found round other stars too. Some giant planets orbit very close to their stars, which no model of our own solar system expected.
Comets and asteroids are leftovers that never grew into planets. Comets are mostly ice and dust, and asteroids are mostly rock and metal.

perspectives.who: Many planet scientists, including James Pollack and his team in 1996
perspectives.explanation: This idea is called core accretion. A core of rock and ice grows first, until it is several times the Earth's weight. Then its gravity pulls in gas from the disc and the planet swells into a giant. This fits Jupiter, which seems to have a heavy centre, and it explains why Uranus and Neptune have more ices.

perspectives.who: Alan Boss, an American astronomer, in 1997
perspectives.explanation: This idea is called disc instability. A thick part of the disc may collapse under its own gravity, all at once, into a giant ball of gas. This could be faster than building a core first. Speed matters, because the gas in a disc disappears within a few million years.

explanations.art: A young Sun in the middle of a flat disc, a dotted circle marking the frost line, small rocky lumps inside it and bigger icy lumps with gas swirling in outside it.
explanations.context: This card gives the best ideas for why our solar system has two kinds of planets. It is a good place to see that scientists agree on part of a story and argue about the rest.

explanations.concept: Inside a rocky planet: a core, a mantle and a crust
explanations.definition: The Earth is made of layers. At the centre is a core of iron and nickel, with a solid inner part and a liquid outer part. Round it is a thick layer of hot rock called the mantle. On the outside is a thin, cool crust.
explanations.description: The Earth's radius is about 6,371 kilometres. The deepest hole people have drilled goes down only about 12 kilometres, so we have never seen the inside. We know it from earthquakes. When the ground shakes, waves travel through the Earth and are picked up by instruments on the other side. Waves bend, speed up, slow down and stop depending on what they pass through. The solid inner core is about 1,220 kilometres in radius. The liquid outer core reaches out to about 3,480 kilometres. The moving metal in the outer core makes the Earth's magnetic field. When the heavy iron sank to the middle long ago, the lighter rock floated above it. That is why the Earth's inside is layered.
examples: A boiled egg is a rough model: the yolk is the core, the white is the mantle and the shell is the crust. The Earth's crust is far thinner compared with its size.
Mars and Mercury also seem to have iron cores. Mercury's core is very large in proportion to the planet.
The Earth's inner core is about as hot as the surface of the Sun, but it stays solid because of the huge pressure squeezing it.
explanations.art: The Earth cut open, with its solid inner core, liquid outer core, mantle and thin crust labelled, and a drill hole that reaches only the very top.
explanations.context: This card explains what is under our feet and how scientists found out without digging.

explanations.concept: Craters work as a clock for the age of a surface
explanations.definition: A surface that has many craters has been exposed to space rocks for a long time, so it is old. A surface with few craters is young, because something has covered or wiped away the older ones.
explanations.description: Space rocks have been hitting the planets for 4.5 billion years. A rock hitting a world digs a bowl-shaped crater, and it is round whichever way the rock came in, because the energy of the hit spreads out in all directions. Bigger and faster rocks dig bigger craters. A new crater that overlaps an old one cuts through it, so you can tell which came first. On the Moon, the bright highlands are covered with craters and are more than 4 billion years old. The dark plains, which are hardened lava, have far fewer craters and are about 3 to 3.5 billion years old. Counting craters per area is how scientists date places they have never touched. The Earth has fewer than 200 known craters, because water, wind, plants and moving crust wipe them away.
examples: Mercury and the Moon are covered with craters because they have almost no air and no rain to wear them down.
Venus has only about 1,000 craters, spread evenly. This tells us its whole surface is young, probably only a few hundred million years old.
Mars has an old, heavily cratered south and a younger, smoother north.
explanations.art: A cratered Moon highland next to a smooth dark Moon plain with few craters, and a magnifying glass over a big old crater cut across by a smaller newer one.
explanations.context: This card explains why craters are used as a clock, which is the idea behind the Crater Tray experiment.

explanations.concept: How old is Lonar Lake, the crater in Maharashtra?
explanations.description: Lonar Lake lies near the town of Lonar in Maharashtra. It fills a round crater about 1.8 kilometres across, dug into hard volcanic rock called basalt. Much of the Moon's dark plains are made of the same kind of rock, which is why scientists study Lonar. The crater was made by a space rock that hit long ago. The lake's salty green water and the thrown-out rock round its rim are still there. But when did it happen? Earlier studies suggested about 50,000 years ago. A later study using the rock's radioactive argon suggested around half a million years. The question matters because it shows how hard it is to date an impact, even when you can walk around the crater.
examples: The tests are done on tiny grains of rock that were melted by the impact. When melted rock cools, its natural radioactive clock starts again from zero.
Lonar is one of very few craters in the world dug into basalt, which makes it a useful practice ground for studying the Moon and Mars.
Temples built around the lake are many centuries old, so people have known the lake for a very long time.

perspectives.explanation: The crater formed about 50,000 years ago. This number is still repeated in many books.

perspectives.who: Fred Jourdan and his team, in 2011
perspectives.explanation: The crater is much older, around 570,000 years. They reached this by dating melted rock from the impact with a method that uses the radioactive gas argon.

explanations.art: A round green lake inside a crater with a low forested rim, small temples on the shore, and a map of India with a dot on Maharashtra.
explanations.context: This card is about a real crater in India and a real disagreement about how old it is.

explanations.concept: Atmospheres: the blanket that sets a planet's heat
explanations.definition: An atmosphere is the gas held round a planet by its gravity. Its thickness and its gases decide how much heat the planet keeps. The greenhouse effect is the trapping of heat by gases such as carbon dioxide.
explanations.description: Sunlight warms a planet's ground. The ground then sends the heat out again. Some gases, such as carbon dioxide and water vapour, slow this heat down on its way out, a bit like a blanket. Mercury has almost no air, so its day side reaches about 430 degrees Celsius and its night side falls to about minus 180. The Earth has a medium air blanket that keeps the average temperature at about 15 degrees Celsius. Without it, the Earth would average about minus 18. Mars has a very thin blanket, less than 1 percent of the Earth's pressure, so it is cold. Venus has a huge blanket, mostly carbon dioxide, pressing on the ground about 90 times harder than the Earth's air. That is why Venus, at about 460 degrees Celsius, is hotter than Mercury.
examples: The air in a closed car in the sun gets hotter than the air outside, because the glass lets sunlight in but slows the heat leaving.
Spacecraft that landed on Venus lasted no more than about two hours before the heat and pressure stopped them.
The Earth's own greenhouse effect makes life possible. Extra carbon dioxide from burning coal and oil makes it stronger and warms the planet more.
explanations.art: Four planets in a row with thermometers beside them showing their average temperatures: Mercury very hot and cold, Venus very hot, the Earth mild, Mars cold, and a blanket of air of different thickness round each.
explanations.context: This card explains why distance from the Sun is not the only thing that decides a planet's temperature.

explanations.concept: Why Mars lost its air and water
explanations.description: Mars has dry river valleys, lake beds and rocks that formed in water. So billions of years ago it was warmer and wetter, with thicker air. Today its air is thin and cold, and its water is mostly ice. Most scientists think Mars lost much of its air to space. Mars is small, so its gravity is weak and holds gas less tightly. Mars also lost its strong magnetic field early. Without that shield, the solar wind, a stream of fast particles from the Sun, could blow the air away bit by bit. NASA's MAVEN spacecraft, which reached Mars in 2014, measured the air escaping to space. So this idea is backed by measurements. But scientists are still working out how much of the loss came from the solar wind and how much from other causes.
examples: The Perseverance rover is exploring a dry river delta in Jezero crater, where a lake once lay.
Mars today has a pale sky and sometimes huge dust storms that cover the whole planet.
Mangalyaan, India's orbiter, carried instruments to study Mars's thin outer air and to look for the gas methane.
explanations.art: Mars long ago with blue water and a thick air, and Mars today dry and red with thin streams of gas drifting off into space on the solar wind.
explanations.context: This card gives the best idea for why Mars changed from a wet world to a dry one. It is an idea that is well supported but not settled.

explanations.concept: Orbits are ellipses, and a planet's year follows a rule
explanations.definition: Every planet moves round the Sun on an ellipse. A planet moves faster when it is closer to the Sun. There is also a rule for the length of its year. Multiply the planet's year by itself. Then work out distance times distance times distance. The two answers are the same, when the year is in Earth years and the distance is in astronomical units.
explanations.description: For about 2,000 years, people believed the planets must move in perfect circles. In 1609, Johannes Kepler, a German astronomer, showed that Mars moves on an oval instead. A few years later he found the rule linking distance and year. For the Earth, both numbers are 1, so the rule is easy to check. Mars is 1.52 astronomical units (AU) from the Sun. 1.52 times 1.52 times 1.52 is about 3.5. Mars's year is 1.88 Earth years. 1.88 times 1.88 is also about 3.5. The rule works for every planet, and for asteroids, comets and planets round other stars. Isaac Newton later showed that it follows from gravity getting weaker with distance. A planet's year is not the same as its day. A year is one trip round the Sun. A day is one spin on its own axis.
examples: Ceres, the largest object in the asteroid belt, is 2.77 AU from the Sun. 2.77 times 2.77 times 2.77 is about 21. So its year, multiplied by itself, must also be about 21. That gives a year of about 4.6 Earth years, and that is Ceres's real year.
A day on Venus lasts 243 Earth days, longer than its year of 225 Earth days. Venus also spins backwards compared with most planets.
Mercury spins on its axis three times for every two trips round the Sun. So from sunrise to sunrise on Mercury takes 176 Earth days.
explanations.art: The Sun at one focus of an oval path with a planet moving fast near the Sun and slow far from it, and a small table showing distance cubed matching year squared.
explanations.context: This card explains the shape of the planets' paths and the rule found by Kepler that links distance and year.

explanations.concept: How big the solar system is: light-minutes and empty space
explanations.definition: Light and radio signals travel at about 300,000 kilometres every second. Even at that speed, crossing the solar system takes minutes to hours. Almost all of the solar system is empty space.
explanations.description: The Earth is 1 astronomical unit from the Sun, and light needs 8 minutes and 20 seconds to cross that distance. So the Sun you see is the Sun of 8 minutes ago. Light takes about 43 minutes to reach Jupiter, and about 4 hours to reach Neptune. A signal to Mars takes between 3 and 22 minutes, depending on where the two planets are in their orbits. A radio message to the Voyager 1 spacecraft, the farthest thing people have sent into space, takes close to a day. So a rover on Mars cannot be driven with a joystick from the Earth. It is given a plan, and it uses its own cameras and computer to avoid danger. In a model with the Sun as a 14-centimetre ball, the Earth is a mustard seed 15 metres away, and Neptune is about 450 metres away. Between the planets there is almost nothing.
examples: When Mangalyaan fired its main engine to enter orbit round Mars in 2014, the signal confirming it took about 12 minutes to reach the Earth.
If the Sun were switched off now, we would see it shining for 8 more minutes and 20 seconds.
In a model where everything is 10 billion times smaller than the real thing, the nearest star after the Sun would be about 4,000 kilometres away. That is further than the length of India.
explanations.art: The Sun at the left with clocks marking the light travel time at each planet, from 3 minutes at Mercury to 4 hours at Neptune, and a tiny spacecraft far to the right.
explanations.context: This card explains how large the solar system is and why signals take so long to cross it.

agreed.text: The four inner planets are small and rocky, and the four outer planets are giants with no solid ground.
agreed.evidence: Spacecraft have landed on Venus and Mars and orbited every planet. Scientists weigh each planet by its pull on its moons or on passing spacecraft, and they measure its size. Together these give its density, which tells rock from gas.

agreed.text: Saturn is less dense than water, and the Earth is the densest planet.
agreed.evidence: Saturn's mass and size have been measured by the Cassini spacecraft, which orbited it for 13 years. Dividing the mass by the volume gives about 0.7 grams in every cubic centimetre, against 1 for water.

agreed.text: The more craters a surface has, the older it is.
agreed.evidence: Rocks that Apollo astronauts brought back from places with many and few craters were dated by their natural radioactivity. The crowded highlands were much older than the smooth plains.

agreed.text: The Earth has a solid inner core inside a liquid outer core.
agreed.evidence: Earthquake waves that pass through the middle of the Earth behave as they would if a solid ball sat inside a liquid shell. This was first suggested in 1936 and later checked with better instruments, with clear proof in 1971.

agreed.text: Venus is hotter than Mercury because of its thick carbon dioxide atmosphere.
agreed.evidence: Spacecraft that landed on Venus measured about 460 degrees Celsius and an air pressure about 90 times the Earth's. Mercury, closer to the Sun, has almost no air to trap heat.

agreed.text: For every planet, year times year equals distance times distance times distance, with the year in Earth years and the distance from the Sun in astronomical units.
agreed.evidence: Kepler found the rule in 1619 from measurements by Tycho Brahe. It has been checked on every planet, on asteroids and comets, and on planets round other stars.

agreed.text: Light and radio signals take minutes to hours to cross the solar system.
agreed.evidence: The speed of light has been measured in laboratories on the Earth. Controllers watch signals from spacecraft arrive at exactly the times that this speed predicts.

challenging.claim: The planets must travel in perfect circles.
challenging.who: Astronomers from ancient Greece until about 1600, including Aristotle, Ptolemy and Copernicus, and Kepler at first
challenging.for: A circle seemed the most perfect shape, and the heavens were thought to be perfect. A circle also matches what we see for most planets, which move on paths very close to circles.
challenging.against: Tycho Brahe measured the position of Mars very carefully. His measurements put Mars off the circle by about a quarter of the width of the Moon. Kepler could not ignore that, and in 1609 he showed that Mars moves on an oval.
challenging.context: This card is about a belief that lasted about 2,000 years and what finally ended it.

challenging.claim: Craters on the Moon are old volcano craters.
challenging.who: Many scientists in the 1800s, and some into the early 1900s
challenging.for: The Moon has volcanic plains, and some volcanoes on the Earth have round craters.
challenging.against: In 1893 Grove Karl Gilbert, an American geologist, argued that Moon craters were made by impacts, and he tested it by shooting clay balls into soft clay. Real volcano craters are mostly at the tops of cones, while Moon craters are shallow bowls with raised rims. In 1960 Eugene Shoemaker found impact-shocked rock at Meteor Crater in Arizona.
challenging.context: This card is about a long argument over where craters come from. The Crater Tray experiment, where you drop a marble into flour, is a small version of Gilbert's experiment.

challenging.claim: Mars has canals built by clever Martians.
challenging.who: Percival Lowell, an American astronomer, in the 1890s and early 1900s
challenging.for: Giovanni Schiaparelli, an Italian astronomer, drew thin lines on Mars in 1877 and called them 'canali', the Italian word for channels. Lowell saw them too and drew many more.
challenging.against: Better telescopes did not show the lines. In 1965 the Mariner 4 spacecraft flew past Mars and photographed a dry, cratered world with no canals. The lines came from the eye joining up faint marks.
challenging.context: This card is about a famous mistake, made by careful people looking through telescopes at the edge of what they could see.

challenging.claim: Venus, the Earth's neighbour of nearly the same size, must be a warm, wet world with jungles.
challenging.who: Many writers and some scientists in the early 1900s
challenging.for: Venus is nearly the Earth's size and is covered in thick white clouds, which could hide swamps.
challenging.against: In 1962 the Mariner 2 spacecraft measured Venus's surface as hotter than an oven. In 1970 the Soviet Venera 7 landed there and sent signals for about 23 minutes from the hot ground.
challenging.context: This card is about a guess based on size alone, and what the spacecraft found.

challenging.claim: A gas giant is a ball of gas all the way down, with no solid centre at all.
challenging.who: Some planet scientists, especially since the Juno spacecraft's results in 2017
challenging.for: Jupiter has no surface, and Juno's gravity measurements suggest a centre that is not a small, sharp ball but a fuzzy, spread-out mix of heavy elements and hydrogen.
challenging.against: Before Juno, many models gave Jupiter a clear, dense core of rock and ice. Some models still do, and the data can be read more than one way.
challenging.context: This card is about what is in the middle of Jupiter, which scientists have not yet settled.

big_questions.q: Venus is almost the same size as the Earth, and yet it is nothing like the Earth. What small differences can make two worlds so different?
big_questions.hint: Think about the air. Venus has a very thick blanket of carbon dioxide and the Earth has a thin one. Where did each get its air?

big_questions.q: Saturn would float in water. Is heaviness something a thing has, or does it depend on how the thing is packed?
big_questions.hint: Think of a steel nut and a steel ship. Both are made of steel. One floats and one sinks.

big_questions.q: The Moon keeps every dent for billions of years, while the Earth wipes most of its dents away. Is a world that erases its past more alive than one that keeps it?
big_questions.hint: Think about what wipes away the Earth's craters: water, wind, plants and moving ground. Are those things alive?

big_questions.q: The light of the Sun reaches us 8 minutes after it leaves. When you look at the Sun, is it 'now' there?
big_questions.hint: A letter takes days to arrive and is already old when you read it. What is different about the light?

big_questions.q: In a model with the Sun as a 14-centimetre ball, the nearest star is 4,000 kilometres away. What is all that space between the stars for?
big_questions.hint: Is empty space really empty? What can pass through it, and what cannot?

big_questions.q: We know of only one planet with life. Is the Earth lucky, or would many worlds like ours happen anyway?
big_questions.hint: How would you find out with just one example? What would you want to count?

big_questions.q: Some scientists once said Jupiter's gravity protects the Earth from comets. Others say it also throws some towards us. How could you test either idea?
big_questions.hint: You cannot run the history of the solar system a second time. What could you do instead, using computer models or craters?

big_questions.q: Jupiter has no surface. So where does the planet stop and space begin?
big_questions.hint: Astronomers pick a level where the pressure matches the Earth's sea level. Is that a fact about Jupiter or a choice people made?

story.title: Twelve Minutes Late
story.note: Kavya, her Thatha and her Amma are made up. The Mars Orbiter Mission, Mangalyaan, is real. It went into orbit round Mars on 24 September 2014, on India's first try. Its main engine burned for about 24 minutes. The signal confirming this took about 12 minutes to reach the Earth. Exact times in the story are rounded. Thatha's work as a telegraph operator is imagined.
text: For a week, Kavya's mother had not slept at home. Amma was an engineer at the space centre in Bengaluru, and the whole team was waiting for one morning. Kavya was nine, and she had stuck a poster of Mars on the wall above her bed.

On that morning she sat in front of the television with her grandfather, Thatha, at six-thirty. Thatha had worked all his life as a telegraph operator, tapping out messages for the railways. He drank his tea slowly and said nothing, which was how he showed he was excited.

A man on the news was speaking. 'Within the hour, Mangalyaan will fire its big engine,' he said. 'It must slow the spacecraft down just enough for Mars to catch it. The engine has not been used for ten months. The burn will last twenty-four minutes.'
'Twenty-four minutes,' said Kavya. 'That is a long time to hold your breath. Thatha, why can't Amma's team watch and press stop, if something goes wrong?'

Thatha put down his glass. 'Ah. I know about that. In my day, a message from Madras to Delhi was not just sent. It was passed, station to station. By the time Delhi answered, the news was old.' He looked at her over his glasses. 'Space is a very long telegraph line, my dear. How long does a message take to reach Mars?'

Kavya did not know. But she had a pencil and the newspaper. Her teacher had told her that light travels three lakh kilometres every second. The man on the television had said Mars was about two hundred and twenty-five million kilometres away that day.

She wrote it as a long division and crossed out the zeros, the way she had been taught. Two hundred and twenty-five million divided by three lakh came to seven hundred and fifty. 'Seven hundred and fifty seconds,' she whispered. She counted on her fingers. 'That is twelve and a half minutes.'
Thatha raised his eyebrows. 'So a message takes twelve and a half minutes to get there. And the answer takes twelve and a half minutes to come back.'

Kavya sat up very straight. 'That is twenty-five minutes. The burn is only twenty-four. If something went wrong in the first minute, Amma would not even see it for twelve minutes, and her stop message would take twelve minutes more. The burn would be over before it arrived.'

'So Mangalyaan has to do it all by itself,' said Kavya slowly. 'They have to tell it everything in advance. It has to decide for itself what to do. Nobody can drive it.' She looked at the television. The man had gone quiet, and a small clock was counting down.

Then the small clock on the screen reached zero. Nobody in the room moved. 'It has started,' whispered Kavya. Thatha shook his head gently. 'No, child. We are looking at old news. The burn began twelve minutes ago. In fact, it may be nearly over.'

Kavya stared at him. Somewhere out there, the engine had already fired. It had either worked or it had not. The answer already existed, travelling towards the Earth like a letter in the post. All the people at the space centre, her mother among them, could do nothing but wait for it to arrive.

They waited for twenty-four more minutes. Thatha's tea went cold. Then the people on the screen jumped to their feet and clapped. The signal had come. Mangalyaan was in orbit round Mars. Kavya screamed, and Thatha, who never raised his voice, laughed out loud.

Amma phoned at nine, hoarse and happy. 'We waited over half an hour for something that had already happened,' she said. 'Did you know the Earth and Mars have a delay?' 'Twelve and a half minutes, Amma,' said Kavya. 'I worked it out on the newspaper.' There was a pause. 'Did you?' said her mother.
Later, Kavya stood at the window. The Sun was high over the neem tree. She remembered that its light, too, had left it eight minutes ago. She waved at it anyway.
story.epiphany: For the parent: light and radio signals travel fast but not instantly. Across the solar system they take minutes to hours, so a message to Mars is old when it arrives, and a spacecraft far away must act on its own. Kavya works out the delay by dividing a distance by a speed. The key idea in the story is that the burn had already succeeded or failed before anyone on the Earth could know. What we see of a faraway place is always a record of the past.
ask: Why could Amma's team not simply press stop if the engine went wrong?
How did Kavya work out that a message to Mars takes about twelve and a half minutes?
When Thatha said 'We are looking at old news', what did he mean?
Why is the Sun you see through the window always a little in the past?

A girl at a table with a pencil and a folded newspaper, writing a long division with many zeros in the margin, and a poster of Mars on the wall behind her.

roots.context: We have looked at craters, layers, air, orbits and the long delays of light. Now we ask what these tell us about what a world is, and about ourselves.

deep_truth.truth: In the Crater Tray experiment, each marble dropped into the flour left a dent, and newer dents cut into older ones. So the dents told you which hit came first. The Moon and Mercury keep their craters for billions of years, but the Earth's rain, wind and moving ground erase most of its craters. So a planet's surface is a record of what has happened to it, and an active planet like the Earth keeps wiping that record and starting again.
deep_truth.habit: We think of a world as a finished object that simply is the way it looks now. But a surface is a record of what has happened to a world, and of how much that world can wipe out and begin again.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Crater Tray experiment, a later crater cut through an earlier one, so the order could be read. When you sifted flour over the tray, the older craters were softened first. On the Moon, the crowded highlands are more than 4 billion years old, while the Earth has fewer than 200 known craters.

three.who_am_i: Your body also keeps a record and renews itself. A scar stays, but most of your skin is replaced over weeks. You live on a planet that does the same with its surface.
three.what_is_life: A world with moving ground, water and living things wipes out its old craters. A living thing also rebuilds itself all the time. Neither the Earth nor a living body stays the same for long.
three.what_is_this_world: Every planet began from one cloud, and each has had a different history. The Moon kept its history. The Earth turned its into soil, seas and living things.

roots.thread: A planet is not only a place. It is also everything that has happened to it, and things are still happening. The Moon is like a diary where every old entry is still there. The Earth is like a diary that keeps being rewritten. Its rain smooths out its craters, its plates carry old rock down and push new rock up, and its living things turn old material into new forms. The Moon keeps its craters only because nothing there changes them. The Earth loses its craters because so much is still going on there. So a surface tells you how active its world still is.

teachings.teaching: The greatness of this world is that someone who was here yesterday is gone today.
teachings.link: The Earth wipes out its craters as it wipes out everything, and keeps changing. Only a world that stays still can keep its past.

teachings.teaching: All conditioned things are impermanent. When one sees this with wisdom, one turns away from suffering.
teachings.link: Even a planet is not permanent. The Moon's craters last a long time, but the Sun, the planets and the Moon itself had a beginning, and will have an end.

teachings.teaching: Who really knows, and who can say here, where this creation came from?
teachings.link: Scientists have a good idea of how the planets formed, but they still argue about the details, such as how the giants grew. The hymn asks the question in the same spirit.

science.text: The more craters a surface has, the older it is. Counting craters is a main way to date planets and moons.
Venus's surface is young, but whether it was renewed all at once or slowly is not agreed.
Whether life exists anywhere else in the solar system, such as under the surface of Mars, is not yet known.

other_view.view: A crater is only a hole made by the laws of physics. Saying that a world 'remembers' or 'forgets' puts a human idea on a lump of rock. The Moon has no history in any deeper sense than a pebble has. A diary needs a writer and a reader, and rock has neither.

practice.title: Leave a mark and watch it fade
practice.say: Find a dusty shelf or a window ledge. Press one finger gently into the dust and make a clear dent. Look at it for a few breaths. Now think of the Moon, where a dent like this stays for billions of years. Then think of the Earth, where wind and rain would wipe it away. Breathe in slowly three times. Notice that you are standing on a world that keeps changing.
practice.kid: Press a finger into some dust. Look at your dent. On the Moon it would stay for ever. On the Earth, wind and rain wipe it away. Breathe slowly three times.

ask: When a world wipes out its craters, is it forgetting, or is it staying alive?
If you could read the Earth's face like the Moon's, what would it tell you about the last billion years?
Is a diary that cannot be rewritten more honest than one that can?
roots.art: The Moon's cratered face and the Earth's smooth blue-and-green face side by side, joined by a thin line, with a hand pressing a fingerprint into dust in the corner.

games.title: Planet Detectives: which world am I?
games.context: This is a clue game. A reader gives a clue about a mystery planet, and everyone guesses which of the eight planets it is, and whether it is rocky or a giant.

setup.art: Twenty-four cards in a face-down pile beside a row of eight numbered spaces, one for each planet in order from the Sun.
setup.caption: 1. Cut out the cards and the planet row. Shuffle the cards into a pile.

setup.art: One child reading a clue card aloud while three others hold their hands behind their backs, ready to count down.
setup.caption: 2. The reader reads a clue. Everyone gets ready to show fingers.

setup.art: Four hands held up together showing 6, 5, 6 and 2 fingers, with the reader turning the card over to show the answer.
setup.caption: 3. On three, everyone shows the planet's number on their fingers. Then the reader turns the card over.

printables.title: A row of 8 spaces, one for each planet in order from the Sun, numbered 1 to 8
24 two-sided cards: a clue about a mystery planet on the front, and the answer on the back

items.f: CLUE. I am the smallest planet. I have almost no air, so I am about 430 degrees Celsius by day and about minus 180 at night.
items.b: Mercury, number 1. Rocky. With no air to hold the heat, it swings from very hot to very cold.

items.f: CLUE. A year on me lasts only 88 Earth days. I move faster than any other planet.
items.b: Mercury, number 1. Rocky. The closest planet to the Sun has the shortest year and moves fastest.

items.f: CLUE. My surface is covered in craters like the Moon's. Ice hides in some craters near my poles, where the Sun never shines.
items.b: Mercury, number 1. Rocky. Craters near the poles are in permanent shadow, so ice can stay frozen there.

items.f: CLUE. I am the hottest planet, at about 460 degrees Celsius. I am not the closest to the Sun.
items.b: Venus, number 2. Rocky. Its thick carbon dioxide air traps heat, so it is hotter than Mercury.

items.f: CLUE. A day on me lasts longer than my year. I also spin backwards compared with most planets.
items.b: Venus, number 2. Rocky. One spin takes 243 Earth days, and one trip round the Sun takes 225.

items.f: CLUE. My air presses on the ground about 90 times harder than the Earth's air. Landers sent to me worked for no more than about two hours.
items.b: Venus, number 2. Rocky. The heat and the pressure on the ground are enough to stop machines.

items.f: CLUE. I am the densest planet, about 5.5 times as dense as water. I have one big moon.
items.b: Earth, number 3. Rocky. The Earth's iron core makes it the densest planet.

items.f: CLUE. Most of my surface is covered by liquid water. My air has oxygen in it, and living things have been here for billions of years.
items.b: Earth, number 3. Rocky. It is the only world we know that has liquid oceans on its surface and life.

items.f: CLUE. Plates of my crust slowly move, making mountains and earthquakes. No other planet is known to have this.
items.b: Earth, number 3. Rocky. Moving plates and wearing water wipe out old craters, so the Earth has few.

items.f: CLUE. I look red because of rusty iron in my dust. A year on me lasts 687 Earth days.
items.b: Mars, number 4. Rocky. Rust gives it the red colour, and it is further out than the Earth, so its year is longer.

items.f: CLUE. My volcano Olympus Mons is about 22 kilometres high, two and a half times as tall as Mount Everest.
items.b: Mars, number 4. Rocky. Mars has solid ground and weak gravity, so its volcanoes grew very tall.

items.f: CLUE. I have dry river valleys and very thin air, mostly carbon dioxide. Two tiny moons go round me.
items.b: Mars, number 4. Rocky. Long ago it was wetter and had thicker air.

items.f: CLUE. I am the biggest planet. More than 1,300 Earths could fit inside me.
items.b: Jupiter, number 5. A gas giant, made mostly of hydrogen and helium.

items.f: CLUE. A storm wider than the Earth has been spinning on me for well over a century. I turn once in less than 10 hours.
items.b: Jupiter, number 5. A gas giant. The Great Red Spot is a giant storm, and Jupiter spins faster than any other planet.

items.f: CLUE. I have no ground. Four of my many moons were found by Galileo in 1610.
items.b: Jupiter, number 5. A gas giant. Galileo saw its four biggest moons with his telescope.

items.f: CLUE. I am so light for my size that I would float in water, if you could find a bathtub big enough.
items.b: Saturn, number 6. A gas giant, with a density of about 0.7. Water is 1.

items.f: CLUE. My bright rings are mostly chunks of water ice, from tiny grains to boulders. They are very wide and very thin.
items.b: Saturn, number 6. A gas giant. The rings are the brightest of any planet.

items.f: CLUE. A year on me lasts about 29 and a half Earth years. I am the second biggest planet.
items.b: Saturn, number 6. A gas giant. It is far from the Sun, so its year is long.

items.f: CLUE. I spin tipped over on my side, so I seem to roll round the Sun. My seasons each last more than 20 years.
items.b: Uranus, number 7. An ice giant. Its year is 84 Earth years and its tilt makes very long seasons.

items.f: CLUE. I was found in 1781 by William Herschel, with his telescope. I am an ice giant, and one of the coldest planets.
items.b: Uranus, number 7. An ice giant. It was the first planet found with a telescope.

items.f: CLUE. Only one spacecraft, Voyager 2, has ever visited me. It flew past in 1986.
items.b: Uranus, number 7. An ice giant. Voyager 2 has also visited Neptune, but not Venus or Mars.

items.f: CLUE. I was found in 1846 by working out with mathematics where to look. I am the farthest planet from the Sun.
items.b: Neptune, number 8. An ice giant. Its pull on Uranus gave away its place.

items.f: CLUE. The fastest winds measured on any planet blow on me, at about 2,000 kilometres an hour. My year is about 165 Earth years.
items.b: Neptune, number 8. An ice giant. Winds blow faster than the speed of sound in the Earth's air.

items.f: CLUE. Sunlight on me is about 900 times weaker than on the Earth. My biggest moon, Triton, goes round me backwards.
items.b: Neptune, number 8. An ice giant. It is 30 times as far from the Sun as the Earth is.

rules: Cut out the 8-space planet row and the 24 cards. Shuffle the cards and put them in a pile with the clue side up.
One player is the reader. The reader takes the top card and reads the clue aloud. The reader does not show the back.
The other players think for a few seconds. Then the reader counts down: 3, 2, 1, show! Everyone holds up as many fingers as the planet's number in the row, from 1 for Mercury to 8 for Neptune.
The reader turns the card over and reads the answer. A player who shows the right number scores 2 points.
A player who also says correctly whether the planet is rocky or a giant, and gives one reason from the clue, scores 1 more point.
The next player to the left becomes the reader. Play 12 cards for a short game, or all 24 for a long one. The player with the most points wins. A tie is a shared win.
Playing alone? Turn up one card at a time, write down your guess, and then check the back. Score yourself, and try to beat your own score the next day.

flow.do: Cut out the planet row and the 24 cards. Shuffle the cards. Put the planet row where everyone can see it.
flow.say: We have eight planets, numbered from the Sun. Mercury is 1 and Neptune is 8. Each card gives a clue about one of them.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Mix them up. Look at the planet row. Mercury is 1.
flow.context: This is the first step of Planet Detectives. You cut out the cards and the planet row.

flow.do: Play the first four cards. After each one, read the answer and talk about which part of the clue gave it away.
flow.say: Read the clue. Count down from three. Show the number on your fingers. Then we check the back. Which word in the clue helped you most?
flow.kid: Listen to the clue. Count down. Show the planet's number. Check the back.
flow.parent: Praise a good reason even when the number is wrong. A child who says 'it must be a giant because it has no ground' is thinking well.

flow.do: Play four more cards. Then stop and ask the question below.
flow.say: Look at the clues for the rocky planets and the clues for the giants. What kinds of clues belong to each?
flow.kid: Think about the clues so far. What kind of clue belongs to a giant?

ask.q: What do the clues for the giants have in common, compared with the clues for the rocky planets?
good: The giants are big, light for their size and have no ground.
The giants have rings and many moons and are far from the Sun.
The rocky planets have craters, volcanoes, or dry land.

check.q: A clue says: 'I am so light for my size that I would float in water.' Is this planet rocky or a giant, and why?
options: A giant, because only gas giants are less dense than water
Rocky, because it floats like a rock
Rocky, because everything light is rocky
check.why: A planet lighter than water must be made mostly of gas, like Saturn. Rock and metal are much denser than water. If you picked 'rocky', you may have thought that rock floats. Try dropping a stone into water.

flow.do: Play the rest of the cards you have time for. Keep score on a piece of paper.
flow.say: Keep going. It is your turn to read the clue. Read it slowly and clearly.
flow.kid: Take turns to be the reader. Keep the score. Try to read each clue clearly.
flow.parent: Younger children can win by getting the number right. Older children can add the rocky or giant answer and a reason.

flow.do: Add up the points. Ask which clue was the hardest and which planet was easiest to spot.
flow.say: Which planet was the easiest to know? Which was the hardest? What made it hard?
flow.kid: Add up your points. Which planet was easiest? Which was hardest?

ask.q: Which kinds of clue were the strongest for telling planets apart?
good: Density, because it tells you rock from gas.
The year, because it tells you the distance.
The air, because it tells you how hot a planet is.

flow.context: This is the last step of Planet Detectives. You count the score and think about which clues helped most.

experiments.title: Crater Tray: what do dents in flour tell us about a world?
experiments.question: When a marble is dropped from higher up, how much wider is the crater it digs? And when one crater lands on another, how can you tell which came first?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. If you drop a marble from 8 times as high, will the crater be 8 times as wide, about twice as wide, or only a little wider? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same marble, the same tray, and flour of the same depth, smoothed flat before every drop. Let the marble fall from a measured height. Never throw it. Only the drop height changes, so any change in the crater comes from the height. Drop three times from each height, because one drop can be a fluke.

materials.item: a deep steel tray or a big plate with a rim, about 30 centimetres across
about 1 kilogram of plain flour (maida or wheat flour), enough to make a layer 3 centimetres deep
2 tablespoons of cocoa powder, ragi flour or fine ground coffee, to dust on top
a tea strainer or a small sieve
a glass marble about 1.5 centimetres across, or any small hard round thing such as a steel ball bearing or a smooth round pebble
a 30 centimetre ruler, a metre scale or tape measure, and a spoon
old newspaper to put under the tray
a pencil and the results table

experiments.safety: Flour dust can make you cough, so do not blow on the tray. Work away from a fan. Keep marbles away from children under five, who might swallow them. Wheat flour is a problem for anyone allergic to wheat or gluten: use rice flour or fine dry sand instead, and wash hands afterwards. If the flour is damp or lumpy, dry it in the sun and sift it first. Do not eat the flour or cocoa from the tray.

schedule.what: Make your guess and prepare the tray. Drop the marble from 10, 20, 40 and 80 centimetres, three times each. Then make three overlapping craters and work out which came first. Last, sift fresh flour over half the tray as 'weather' and see how the craters soften.

experiments.record: Fill in the results table. Then draw a bar chart with one bar for each height, using the average width. Sketch the three overlapping craters and write which came first.
experiments.context: In this experiment you make craters in flour with a marble. You find out how the size of a crater changes with the speed of the hit, and how to read which crater is oldest.

setup.art: A steel tray on newspaper filled with flour about 3 centimetres deep, being smoothed flat with the edge of a ruler.
setup.caption: 1. Fill the tray with 3 centimetres of flour. Smooth it flat with a ruler.

setup.art: A hand sprinkling a thin layer of dark cocoa powder through a tea strainer over the pale flour.
setup.caption: 2. Dust a thin layer of cocoa powder over the top.

setup.art: A child holding a marble between finger and thumb at the 40 centimetre mark of a vertical metre scale beside the tray.
setup.caption: 3. Hold the marble at the first height. Let go. Do not throw it.

setup.art: A ruler laid across a round crater in the flour showing its width from rim to rim, with the marble sitting at the bottom.
setup.caption: 4. Measure the width of the crater from rim to rim. Then lift out the marble.

setup.art: Three craters in the flour that overlap each other, the smallest cutting into the edge of the biggest, with a sieve dusting fresh flour above them.
setup.caption: 5. Make three overlapping craters, then sift on some 'weather' and compare.

flow.do: Show your child the tray, the marble and the ruler. Ask for the guess and the reason. Write both down at the top of the table.
flow.say: The marble is a rock from space. The flour is the ground of a planet. If I drop the marble from 8 times as high, how much wider will the crater be? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: The marble is a space rock. If you drop it from 8 times as high, how much wider will the crater be? Guess. Say why.

ask.q: Why do you think the crater will be that much wider?
good: A faster rock hits harder, so it digs more.
Eight times as high should make a crater eight times as wide.
The crater will not change much, because the marble is the same.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Many children say 8 times as wide. That is a natural idea, and the tray will answer it.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Crater Tray test. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Put the tray on newspaper. Pour in flour to 3 centimetres deep. Shake the tray gently, and smooth the top with the edge of the ruler. Dust a thin layer of cocoa powder over it with the strainer.
flow.say: This is our planet's ground. We make it flat and smooth. The dark cocoa on top will show where the flour is thrown out.
flow.kid: Fill the tray with flour. Make it flat. Sprinkle a little cocoa on top.
flow.parent: If the flour feels damp, spread it on a plate in the sun for an hour first. Damp flour makes steep, sticky craters that fall in. The layer should look like fresh snow, with no marks on it.
flow.context: In this step you make the planet's ground ready for the first drop.

flow.do: Stand a metre scale beside the tray. Hold the marble at 10 centimetres above the flour and let go. Lay the ruler across the crater and read its width from rim to rim. Lift the marble out with a spoon. Smooth the flour, dust it again, and repeat. Do 3 drops at 10 centimetres, then 3 at 20, 3 at 40 and 3 at 80.
flow.say: Hold the marble high, then let it go. Do not push it. Read the width across the middle. Write the number down. Then smooth the flour again.
flow.kid: Drop the marble from 10 centimetres. Measure the crater. Smooth the flour. Do it three times.
flow.parent: With one child: the child drops and measures, and you smooth the flour and write the numbers. With 2 to 4 children: one drops, one measures, one smooths and dusts, and one writes. They swap jobs after each height. If you have two trays, each pair of children can run its own. Expect the craters to grow slowly. At 10 centimetres the crater may be about 3 centimetres wide, and at 80 centimetres about 4.5. These are typical results only. Your numbers may differ by a centimetre or so, and a damp tray or a different marble will change them. What matters is the pattern. Measure from the top of the rim on one side to the top of the rim on the other.

check.q: A marble dropped from 8 times as high hits the flour faster. Its crater was only about one and a half times as wide. What does this tell you?
options: A faster hit makes a wider crater, but only a little wider
The speed of the hit makes no difference to the width
The crater becomes exactly 8 times as wide
check.why: The widths did go up each time, so speed matters. But the crater grew only a little. Saying that speed makes no difference ignores the numbers. 'Exactly 8 times as wide' is the natural guess, but the tray did not show it.

flow.do: Smooth and dust the flour again. Turn your back. Your grown-up drops the marble three times in three nearby spots from the same height, so each crater overlaps the one before. They keep the order secret. Now turn round and look at the craters. Decide which came first, second and third.
flow.say: I made three craters, one after another, and they overlap. Look at the edges. Where one crater cuts into another, which is newer? Which is the oldest?
flow.kid: Your grown-up makes three overlapping craters in secret. Look at the edges. Which came first?

check.q: Crater A has a complete round rim. Crater B's rim cuts into A, so a piece of A's rim is missing. Which crater is older?
options: Crater A, because B cut into it
Crater B, because it cuts into A
You cannot tell which is older
check.why: A new crater destroys part of whatever it lands on, so the crater with the broken rim is the older one. The complete one is the newer. Scientists use the same rule on the Moon. If you picked 'cannot tell', look at which rim is complete.

flow.parent: Make the second crater overlap the edge of the first and the third overlap the edge of the second. Do not hide the marble in your fist. Tell your child the true order after they decide.

flow.do: Take the sieve and shake a thin layer of fresh flour over half of the tray. This is the 'weather'. Leave the other half alone. Compare the craters in the two halves.
flow.say: Half of this tray has had weather. Look at the craters in each half. Which craters are sharper? Which are softer? What could the Earth do that the Moon cannot?
flow.kid: Sift some flour over half the tray. Look at both halves. Which craters are sharper?

ask.q: On the Earth, what kinds of weather wipe out craters?
good: Rain washes the sides down.
Wind carries dust that fills them in.
Plants grow in them and rivers fill them up.

flow.parent: The craters under the flour layer will look softer and shallower, and the oldest craters will fade first. This is the same reason the Earth has so few craters and the Moon has so many.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see in the tray? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things: what you think now, what you saw, and why you think it happened.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: a faster rock digs a wider crater, but only a little wider, and the order of craters can be read. What I saw: from 10 centimetres the average was about 3 centimetres and from 80 centimetres about 4.5. A crater with a cut rim was older. Why: a hit throws flour out in all directions, and a later hit destroys whatever is in its way. The Moon has no weather, so it keeps every crater. Counting craters is how scientists date a surface.

experiments.title: Two Tumblers in the Sun: does a lid make a hotter world?
experiments.question: Does ice melt faster in a tumbler with a clear lid than in an open tumbler, when both sit in the same sunshine?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Two tumblers with ice sit in the sun, one open and one covered with clear film. Which ice will melt first? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use two tumblers of the same kind, the same number of ice cubes of the same size from the same tray, and the same dark paper under each. Put them side by side in the same sunny spot, at the same time. Only the lid changes. Check every 5 minutes with the same clock, and also note the minute the last piece of ice disappears in each tumbler.
results_table: Open tumbler: how much ice is left? (all, half, little, none)
Covered tumbler: how much ice is left? (all, half, little, none)

materials.item: 2 clear glass or plastic tumblers of the same kind
6 ice cubes of the same size from one tray (3 for each tumbler)
clear cling film and a rubber band, enough to cover one tumbler
2 pieces of black or dark paper to stand the tumblers on
a sunny windowsill, balcony wall or terrace table in direct sun
a phone or clock for timing, and a notebook
a digital fever thermometer (optional; it reads only above about 32 degrees Celsius)

experiments.safety: A grown-up must be there if the test is on a balcony or terrace. Keep tumblers away from the edge. Do not touch a tumbler that has been in strong sun without checking that it is not hot. Plastic tumblers are safer than glass. Never look straight at the Sun.

schedule.what: Make your guess. Put three ice cubes in each tumbler, cover one with film, and place both in the sun. Check every 5 minutes. Repeat once if you have time.

experiments.record: Fill in the results table. Draw the two tumblers at the end of the test. Write which melted first and by how many minutes.
experiments.context: In this experiment you put ice in two tumblers, one covered and one open, in the same sunshine. It is a small model of why a blanket of air makes a planet hotter.

setup.art: Two identical tumblers standing on two squares of black paper, each with three ice cubes inside.
setup.caption: 1. Put three ice cubes in each tumbler on dark paper.

setup.art: One tumbler stretched over with clear cling film held tight by a rubber band, next to an open one.
setup.caption: 2. Cover one tumbler with cling film. Leave the other open.

setup.art: Both tumblers side by side on a sunny windowsill, with a phone timer and a notebook beside them.
setup.caption: 3. Place both in the sun, side by side, and start the timer.

setup.art: The open tumbler with a puddle and no ice, the covered tumbler with a small piece of ice still floating.
setup.caption: 4. Check every 5 minutes. Write how much ice is left in each.

flow.do: Show your child the two tumblers and the film. Ask for a guess and a reason. Write it down.
flow.say: One tumbler has a clear lid and one does not. Both sit in the same sunshine. Which ice melts first? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: One tumbler is covered. One is open. Which ice melts first? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think that one will melt first?
good: The lid keeps the heat in.
The open one has more air going past it.
They will melt at the same time, because the sun is the same.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Two Tumblers test. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Stand the two tumblers on the black paper. Put three ice cubes in each. Stretch cling film over one tumbler. Hold it with a rubber band. Carry both to the sunny spot together.
flow.say: The black paper soaks up sunlight, so the tumblers get a good share of it. The film is our blanket of air. Carry them out together, side by side.
flow.kid: Put ice in both tumblers. Cover one with film. Carry both into the sun.
flow.parent: Take the ice straight from the freezer and set up quickly, so the ice has not already started melting. Place the tumblers an arm's length apart, so one does not shade the other. With one child: the child watches both tumblers and you keep time. With 2 to 4 children: one child looks after each tumbler, one keeps the clock and one writes. Two tumblers are enough for any group.
flow.context: In this step you set up both tumblers in the same sunshine.

flow.do: Start the timer. Every 5 minutes, look at both tumblers. Write down how much ice is left in each: all, half, little or none. Keep going until the ice in both has melted, or until 30 minutes have passed.
flow.say: Look closely at both tumblers. How much ice is left in each? Write it down. We check again in 5 minutes.
flow.kid: Every 5 minutes, look at both. How much ice is left? Write it down.
flow.parent: Choose a bright day around noon. A cloudy or rainy day will not work, so if there is no direct sun today, try another day. Expect the ice in the covered tumbler to melt a little sooner, often by a few minutes. Droplets inside the film are normal. If both seem equal, repeat the test with 4 cubes each, or on a hotter, sunnier day. If the covered ice melts later, say so honestly, and check that the film did not touch the ice or shade it. The result can be small, and a small difference is still a finding.

flow.do: If you have a fever thermometer, wait until the ice has gone. Then push its tip into the air space of each tumbler. Read the number and write it down. Then talk about what you saw.
flow.say: Which melted first? How much sooner? Is that enough to be sure, or could it be a fluke? How could we find out?
flow.kid: Which ice melted first? By how many minutes? Could we try it again?

check.q: The ice in the covered tumbler melted sooner. What is the best reason?
options: The film kept the warm air from escaping, so the air inside got hotter
The film made more sunshine
The ice in the covered tumbler was a different kind
check.why: Sunlight passes through the clear film and warms the paper and the air. The film stops the warm air from flowing away, so the inside gets hotter. The film does not make sunshine, and a fair test uses the same ice. If you picked 'a different kind', check that you used cubes from the same tray.

flow.parent: A digital fever thermometer reads only above about 32 degrees Celsius. Stop if it shows HI.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three things: what they think now, what they saw, and why they think it happened. Then tell your child how this is like Venus.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see? Why do you think it happened? Venus is like the covered tumbler, with a thick blanket of air round it.
flow.kid: Say or write three things: what you think now, what you saw, and why you think it happened.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: a cover makes things warmer. What I saw: the covered tumbler's ice melted first, by a few minutes (your gap may be larger or smaller). Why: the film stopped warm air from leaving. Be honest that this is only a model. A lid stops warm air from rising away. On Venus, the gas carbon dioxide slows down heat rays on their way out. The two work differently in detail, but both act like a blanket.

activities.title: Walk the Solar System: the Sun is a disc 14 centimetres wide

materials.item: a sheet of card, scissors and a pencil, to cut a Sun disc 14 centimetres across

small things for the planets: a pinch of pepper powder, 2 mustard seeds, a grain of salt, a small marble or bead, a bead or small marble a little smaller, and 2 peppercorns. Keep these small things away from children under five. Stick the pepper powder and salt to a dab of glue or sticky tape.
8 slips of paper, tape and a pen, for labels
a measuring tape or a long string marked in metres
a long corridor, hall or terrace of about 25 metres, and if possible an open ground or a quiet road for the outer planets
a map of India, in an atlas or on a phone

schedule.what: Guess how far the Earth should be from the Sun. Make the Sun and the planets to the same scale. Measure your step. Walk to Mercury, Venus, the Earth and Mars. Work out where the giants would be.

activities.record: Make a table with each planet, its size in this model, its distance in metres and its distance in your steps. Draw the row of planets with the Sun, and mark how far away the nearest star would be.
activities.context: In this activity you build a model of the solar system where the sizes and the distances are both shrunk by the same amount. It shows how small the planets are and how far apart.

setup.art: A round card disc 14 centimetres wide labelled Sun, next to a tape measure, and a mustard seed on a paper slip labelled Earth.
setup.caption: 1. Cut a Sun disc 14 centimetres wide. Tape a mustard seed to a slip for the Earth.

setup.art: A child counting steps beside a measuring tape laid on the floor to find the length of one step.
setup.caption: 2. Measure how long your step is.

setup.art: A long corridor with the Sun disc at one end and four tiny labelled seeds taped to the floor at different distances, the Earth about 30 steps away.
setup.caption: 3. Walk out from the Sun and place each planet at its distance.

setup.art: A map of India with a long arrow from Kanyakumari to Kashmir and beyond, and a small star at the end labelled nearest star.
setup.caption: 4. At this scale, the nearest star is further away than the whole length of India.

flow.do: Show your child the 14 centimetre Sun disc. Explain that the Earth is a mustard seed in this model. Ask for a guess on how far away the Earth should be, in steps.
flow.say: Here is the Sun, 14 centimetres wide. The Earth is this mustard seed, about 1 millimetre wide. How many steps from the Sun do you think the seed should go? Why?
flow.kid: Here is the Sun. The Earth is a seed. How many steps away should the seed go? Guess. Why?

ask.q: Why do you think that many steps?
good: The Sun is far from the Earth, so a lot of steps.
The seed is tiny, so the Earth must be a long way off.
Maybe five steps, because the planets are drawn close in books.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Most people guess a few steps. The real answer is about 30 steps for a child.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Walk the Solar System activity. You guess how far apart the Sun and the Earth should be.

flow.do: Cut a Sun disc 14 centimetres wide. Tape each planet to a slip of paper and write its name. Then walk 10 steps along a tape measure and read how far you went. Divide by 10 to find the length of one step.
flow.say: In this model, 1 millimetre stands for 10,000 kilometres. So the Sun is 14 centimetres, the Earth is about 1 millimetre, and Jupiter is 14 millimetres. Now find how long your step is.
flow.kid: Make the Sun and the planets. Walk 10 steps and measure how far you went. Divide by 10 to get the length of one step.
flow.parent: A grown-up helps with the scissors. With one child: the child walks and counts, and you tape the planets down. With 2 to 4 children: one walks and counts steps, one holds the tape, one places and labels the planets, and one writes the table. All take turns being the walker. Each child can make a different planet. Sizes in this model: Mercury 0.5 millimetres, a pinch of pepper powder. Venus 1.2 and the Earth 1.3 millimetres, mustard seeds. Mars 0.7, a grain of salt. Jupiter 14 millimetres, a marble. Saturn 12, a smaller bead. Uranus and Neptune 5 each, peppercorns. A child's step is about 50 centimetres, so 2 steps make a metre.
flow.context: In this step you make the model and measure your step.

flow.do: Put the Sun disc at one end of the corridor. Walk away from it and count your steps. Tape down Mercury at 5.8 metres, Venus at 10.8, the Earth at 15 and Mars at 22.8. Then look back at the Sun from Mars. Write the steps in the table.
flow.say: At 50 centimetres a step, Mercury is about 12 steps away. Venus is about 22, the Earth about 30 and Mars about 46. Look back at the Sun from Mars. How big does it look? Can you see the seed?
flow.kid: Walk out from the Sun. Tape the planets down at their distances. Look back at the Sun.

ask.q: What surprised you about the space between the planets?
good: How far apart they are.
How tiny the planets are next to the Sun.
That there is nothing but empty floor in between.

flow.parent: Most homes are shorter than 25 metres, so a terrace, a school ground, a park path or a flat roof is better than a corridor. If you only have a short corridor, do Mercury, Venus and the Earth, and calculate Mars. For the outer planets, the distances are Jupiter 78 metres, Saturn 143 metres, Uranus 287 metres and Neptune 450 metres. That is like 4 cricket pitches to Jupiter, and about 4 football grounds in a row to Neptune. You can walk these beside a quiet road or on a school ground, if you have one. Go with your child, and keep off the road and away from traffic.

flow.do: Remind your child that the Earth is 15 metres from the Sun in this model. Tell them the nearest star after the Sun would be about 4,000 kilometres away. Ask where that would be, using a map of India.
flow.say: In this model the nearest other star is about 4,000 kilometres away. India is about 3,200 kilometres long, from Kashmir to Kanyakumari. So that star is further than the whole length of India. What is in all that space?
flow.kid: The nearest star would be 4,000 kilometres away. That is more than the length of India!

check.q: In the model, the Sun is a 14-centimetre disc and the Earth is a seed 15 metres away. What does this tell you about the solar system?
options: Most of the solar system is empty space, with tiny planets very far apart
The planets are close together and about the size of the Sun
The Earth is almost touching the Sun
check.why: The Earth is a speck, and the space between the Sun and the Earth is huge. The same is true for every planet. If you pictured planets close together, you may be thinking of book pictures, which squeeze the planets to fit a page.

flow.do: Ask your child to draw the row of planets from the Sun, with distances. Ask what they would tell a friend who has only seen book pictures.
flow.say: What would you tell a friend who thinks the planets are close together, the way books draw them?
flow.kid: Draw your row of planets. What would you tell a friend about the space between them?

ask.q: What would you tell your friend?
good: The planets are tiny and far apart.
Space is mostly empty.
Book pictures squeeze the planets close to fit on a page.

activities.title: Planet Data Detective: the rule linking distance and year

materials.item: a phone calculator
a notebook and a pencil
the table of distances and years given in the steps (written out by a grown-up)

schedule.what: Guess whether a planet 4 times as far from the Sun has a year 4 times as long. Test two ideas on real data. Find the rule. Use it to predict the year of Ceres.

activities.record: A table with each planet's distance, year, the result of Test 1 and the result of Test 2. Write down which test worked, and the year you predicted for Ceres.
